adults.title: Words That Make Peace
adults.big_idea: Following Jesus Christ includes giving up harsh language and choosing words that bring His peace, and that change begins in the heart.
adults.objective: Learners will name one expression they will stop using and one peacemaking phrase they will start using this week, and will feel that the Savior can change their hearts and their words.
prepare: Read Elder Kyungu’s talk, marking the two lists of expressions (paragraphs 12 and 13) and his closing invitations.
Pray about one relationship of your own where your words could bring more peace.
Bring paper and pens for everyone.
Write on the board before class: Forgo. Replace.

segments.name: Words we still remember
steps: After the opening prayer, ask everyone to think silently for 30 seconds of a sentence someone once said to them that they still remember years later. It may have been kind or it may have hurt. No one needs to share the sentence itself.
Ask the first question below and take two or three answers.
Explain that Elder Alfred Kyungu of the Seventy spent his whole message on this subject, in answer to an invitation President Oaks gave in April 2026.
questions: Without telling us the words, what does it teach you that you still remember them?

segments.name: A call from the prophet
steps: Have someone read President Oaks’s invitation, quoted in the talk (first aligned quote).
Read Elder Kyungu’s comment on it (first key quote).
Discuss the questions. Let the class do the talking; you do not need to add much.
questions: What is the difference between treating this as a suggestion and treating it as a call to discipleship?
Why do you think President Oaks named our families and personal relationships in particular?

segments.name: Forgo and replace
steps: Point to the board. Elder Kyungu called it a spiritual exercise to identify the expressions we need to forgo and then replace them with words that bring peace.
Do not read his whole list of damaging expressions aloud. Simply note that it includes phrases such as “You never listen” and “Leave me alone,” and read what he says such words do (second key quote).

Form groups of three or four. Give each group the list of peacemaking phrases from paragraph 13 (on phones, or read it to them slowly). Each group picks the two phrases that would change the most in a home or a ward, and tells why.
Hand out paper. Allow two quiet minutes for each person to write privately: one expression I need to forgo, and one phrase from Elder Kyungu’s list I will use in its place.
questions: Which of these peacemaking phrases is hardest for you to say, and why?
When has someone’s gentle word changed the direction of a hard conversation for you?

segments.name: The heart behind the words
steps: Divide the room in half. One half reads Matthew 12:34–37; the other reads Ephesians 4:29 and Colossians 4:6. Each half reports in one sentence what the Lord asks of our speech.
Read Alma 24:19 together. Elder Kyungu taught that as the converted Lamanites “buried the weapons of war, for peace,” we too can bury the language of contention.
Read the third key quote. Point out where he says the power to change our language comes from.
Share President Uchtdorf’s sentence (second aligned quote) and ask the last question.
questions: If our words come from what fills our hearts, what does that suggest about where to begin?
What did it cost the converted Lamanites to bury their weapons? What might it cost us to bury a habit of speech?
How has drawing closer to the Savior changed the way you speak to someone?

segments.name: Try it once
steps: Give this made-up situation: two people who love each other disagree about a decision, and voices are starting to rise.
In pairs, each person says aloud one sentence from Elder Kyungu’s list that could be spoken next, such as “Let us slow down and talk” or “I don’t want this to divide us.”
Ask one or two people how it felt to say the words out loud.

segments.name: Invitation and promise
steps: Read Elder Kyungu’s three invitations from paragraph 16 (see invitations): to repent, to pray, and to use language that uplifts.
Read the Savior’s promise in John 14:27 and Elder Kyungu’s witness that this peace is real and begins with our hearts, our choices, and our words.
Invite each person to look again at what they wrote and choose one of the ways to act. Bear your testimony that Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace.
Follow up: tell the class that next week you will begin by asking who used their replacement phrase and what happened.

key_quotes.text: It is not a simple suggestion; it is a call to discipleship as we follow Jesus Christ.
Such words never edify. They weaken love, diminish respect, and damage relationships.
let us fill our hearts with the true doctrine of Christ, which has the power to change our language and help us speak more as peacemakers today, tomorrow, and always.
This peace is real. It is powerful, and it begins with us—with our hearts, our choices, and our words.

scriptures.use: Half the class reads it silently and reports in one sentence what the Savior teaches about where words come from and why they matter.
The other half reads it with Colossians 4:6 and reports what kind of speech Paul asks of the Saints.
Read together; ask what it cost the converted Lamanites to bury their weapons and what it might cost us to bury a habit of speech.
Read aloud at the close as the Savior’s promise attached to the invitation.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: My brothers and sisters, as followers of Christ, let us follow Him by forgoing contention and by using the language and methods of peacemakers. In our families and other personal relationships, let us avoid what is harsh and hateful.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Uchtdorf
aligned_quotes.text: The closer we come to Him, the closer we will come to each other

invitations.text: Let us repent for the harsh language and expressions that have offended our friends, leaders, family members, or colleagues.
Let us pray for peaceful communication among us, regardless of the difference in our opinions.
Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.

takeaways: The prophet’s invitation to speak as a peacemaker is a call to discipleship.
I can identify the words I need to forgo and replace them with words that bring peace.
As I fill my heart with the doctrine of Christ, He changes my language and gives me His peace.
act: Use your chosen replacement phrase at least once a day this week, starting at home.
Go to one person your words have hurt and say, “I’m sorry. Please forgive me.”
Each morning, pray by name for peaceful communication with one person you disagree with.
Before sending a message or post written in frustration, wait, reread it, and ask whether it uplifts.
music: Where Can I Turn for Peace?
adapt: At home: do the forgo-and-replace writing as a family or couple, then post one shared replacement phrase where everyone will see it.
Short on time: keep the opening, the forgo-and-replace segment, and the invitation and promise.
Large class: have people talk with the person beside them instead of forming groups, and take only two reports.

youth.title: Bury It, Replace It
youth.big_idea: Disciples of Jesus Christ drop words that tear down and choose words that bring peace, and He can change our hearts so that those words come naturally.
youth.objective: Youth will rewrite a real-life harsh reply into a peacemaker’s reply and will choose one specific change to make in how they talk or text this week.
prepare: Read Elder Kyungu’s talk. Copy onto separate slips these short phrases from his two lists: “You never listen.” “This is all your fault.” “Just stop talking.” “I do not care.” “Leave me alone.” “I’m sorry.” “We can work this out.” “I am here for you.” “Let us start again.” “I respect your view.” “You are not alone.” “That matters to me.” Make one set for each team.
Write the four situations from the rewrite segment on the board or on cards.
Bring paper and pens. Ask youth to have scriptures or phones ready for the scripture search.
Label two spots on a table or the floor: Builds and Breaks.

segments.name: Sixty-second sort
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, split into two or three teams and hand each a shuffled set of slips. On your signal they race to sort every slip under Builds or Breaks.
When a team finishes, ask everyone the question below. Take quick answers.
Tell them every phrase came from one conference talk: Elder Alfred Kyungu listed words that damage relationships and words that bring peace.
questions: Which one of these have you heard this week? You do not have to say who said it.

segments.name: Why a prophet talked about this
steps: Have a youth read President Oaks’s April 2026 invitation, which Elder Kyungu quoted (first aligned quote).
Have another read Elder Kyungu’s response (first key quote).
Ask the questions. Accept honest answers, including disagreement, and thank them for it.
questions: With everything a prophet could say to the whole world, why do you think he chose how we talk to each other?
Where is it hardest to talk like a peacemaker: at home, at school, in a game, or online? Why there?

segments.name: Scripture search
steps: In pairs, with scriptures or phones: half the pairs take Matthew 12:34–37, the others take Ephesians 4:29.
Each pair writes a summary of its passage in six words or fewer. Give them two minutes, then have each pair read its summary. Let the class vote for the one that says the most with the least.
Read the second key quote. Point out that Elder Kyungu does not only say to try harder; he says the doctrine of Christ has power to change our language.
questions: The Savior said the mouth speaks from what fills the heart. So what is a harsh comment really telling us?
Does this still count if I was just joking? What do these verses suggest?

segments.name: Rewrite the reply
steps: Give each team one made-up situation: (1) a group chat starts mocking someone who is not in it; (2) someone borrows your things without asking, again; (3) a teammate blames you for a loss in front of everyone; (4) a friend strongly disagrees with you about something you care about.
Each team writes two replies: the one that would be easy to send or say, and a peacemaker’s reply that uses at least one phrase from Elder Kyungu’s list (leave the Builds slips out for reference).
Read the fourth key quote, then have teams act out the peacemaker’s reply in under 30 seconds each. Keep it light; laughter is fine.

Ask the questions. Note that Elder Kyungu asks for peaceful communication regardless of differences of opinion, and that his list includes “I respect your view” and “Let us slow down and talk.” Peacemakers still say what they think; they choose how.
questions: Was the peacemaker’s reply weaker or stronger than the easy one? Why?
How can you disagree with someone and still keep peace?

segments.name: Bury it
steps: Read Alma 24:19 together. Elder Kyungu taught that as the converted Lamanites “buried the weapons of war, for peace,” we too can bury the language of contention.
Hand out paper. In silence, each person writes one phrase, tone, or habit (spoken or typed) they want to bury, then folds the paper. No one will read it; they take it home or throw it away.

Read Elder Kyungu’s invitation to repent (see invitations). Say gently that all of us have said things we regret, and that repentance is how the Savior helps us change. Share President Oaks’s words, which Elder Rasband quoted (second aligned quote).

segments.name: One-week challenge
steps: Read the third key quote and the Savior’s promise in John 14:27. Elder Kyungu also taught that as we follow Jesus Christ we will feel His peace.
Invite each person to choose one item from the ways to act and tell a partner which one.
Bear a brief testimony that Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace and that He helps us change.
Follow up: next week, open by asking who used a replacement phrase, where, and what happened. Send one mid-week reminder if your class has a group message.

key_quotes.text: It is not a simple suggestion; it is a call to discipleship as we follow Jesus Christ.
let us fill our hearts with the true doctrine of Christ, which has the power to change our language and help us speak more as peacemakers today, tomorrow, and always.
This peace is real. It is powerful, and it begins with us—with our hearts, our choices, and our words.
We must choose language that strengthens confidence and preserves relationships.

scriptures.use: Half the pairs read it and write a summary in six words or fewer; then discuss what a harsh comment shows about the heart.
The other pairs read it and write a summary in six words or fewer; compare with the Builds slips.
Read together before the silent writing; ask what the youth could bury for peace.
Read at the close as the Savior’s promise of peace.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: let us follow Him by forgoing contention and by using the language and methods of peacemakers. In our families and other personal relationships, let us avoid what is harsh and hateful.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks, quoted by Elder Rasband
aligned_quotes.text: Let us avoid what is harsh and hateful. Let us seek to be holy, like our Savior.

invitations.text: let us use words that encourage understanding and peace
Let us repent for the harsh language and expressions that have offended our friends, leaders, family members, or colleagues.
Let us pray for peaceful communication among us, regardless of the difference in our opinions.

takeaways: How I talk and text is part of following Jesus Christ.
I can bury words that tear down and replace them with words that bring peace.
The Savior can change my heart, and my words will follow.
act: Pick one phrase from the Builds pile and use it out loud every day for seven days.
For one week, before you send a reply written while annoyed, wait one minute and reread it.
Say or send a sincere “I’m sorry” to one person your words have hurt.
Pray each night this week for peace with one person you often clash with.
adapt: At home: do the rewrite activity with situations from your own family life, chosen together, and let the youth lead the acting.
Very small class: skip teams. Sort the slips together and write the replies as one group.
Short on time: keep the sort, the rewrite, and the one-week challenge.

children.title: Peace Words
children.big_idea: Jesus wants me to use kind words that bring peace.
children.objective: Children will say and practice at least one peace word, such as “Please,” “Thank you,” or “I’m sorry,” and will feel that kind words help them follow Jesus.
prepare: Bring building blocks (or small boxes), a soft ball, a blanket, paper, and crayons.
Bring a picture of the Savior.
Choose four peace words from Elder Kyungu’s talk to use all lesson long: “Please.” “Thank you.” “I’m sorry.” “I care about you.”
Read Alma 24:19 so you can tell it simply in your own words.

segments.name: Sing and feel
steps: Sing “Kindness Begins with Me” together, with simple hand actions if you like.
Ask the question and let several children answer.
Say: Today we will learn about peace words. Peace words are kind words that help people feel calm, safe, and loved.
questions: How do you feel inside when someone says something kind to you?

segments.name: Kind words build
steps: Put the blocks in the middle. Say: Kind words build. Let’s see.
Each child takes a turn saying one of the four peace words and adds a block. Build a tower or a bridge together. Help little ones by whispering a word to them.
When it is built, say: Look what kind words can build. Words that hurt can knock things down, so we choose words that build.
Have the children repeat after you: I can use words that bring peace.

segments.name: Jesus and His prophet
steps: Show the picture of the Savior. Say: Jesus is called the Prince of Peace. He wants us to have peace.
Say: Our prophet, President Oaks, asked us to talk like peacemakers. At general conference, Elder Kyungu taught that peace begins with our hearts, our choices, and our words.
Teach the actions: hands on heart (hearts), finger to the side of the head (choices), hands open by the mouth (words). Do it three times together, a little faster each time.
Say the truth again together: I can use words that bring peace.
questions: Who can show me the three places where peace begins?

segments.name: Bury it for peace
steps: Tell the story simply: Long ago, some people in the Book of Mormon learned about Jesus and loved Him. They wanted peace. So they dug a deep hole and buried their weapons in the ground. Elder Kyungu said we can bury unkind words the same way.
Give each child a paper and one crayon. Have them make a quick grumpy scribble. Say: This scribble stands for words that hurt.
Crumple the papers. Walk together, digging with pretend shovels, to the blanket, and bury every paper under it.
Pat the blanket down and say together: We bury unkind words. We choose peace.

segments.name: Peace word ball
steps: Sit or stand in a circle. Roll or gently toss the ball to a child and give a pretend moment: someone bumps into your blocks; a friend looks sad; you want a turn with a toy; someone shares with you; you said something unkind and feel bad about it.
The child holding the ball says a peace word that fits, and everyone repeats it. Then that child rolls the ball back.
Go around until every child has had at least one turn. Praise each answer.
questions: What peace word could you say?

segments.name: Draw my peace word
steps: Give each child a fresh paper. Ask them to draw themselves saying a peace word to someone.
As they draw, go to each child and ask which peace word they will use this week. Write it on their paper.
Invite them to put the picture where they will see it and to show it to someone at home.

segments.name: Jesus gives peace
steps: Hold up the picture of the Savior again. Say: Jesus promised to give us His peace. When we use peace words, we are following Him.

Share Elder Soares’s words, which Elder Kyungu quoted (see aligned quotes), in simple terms: we can be helpers who bring Jesus’s peace to others. Bear a one-sentence testimony that Heavenly Father loves us and wants us to live in peace.
Sing one verse of the song I’m Trying to Be like Jesus and close with prayer.
Follow up: next week, start by asking each child which peace word they said and to whom.

key_quotes.text: This peace is real. It is powerful, and it begins with us—with our hearts, our choices, and our words.
let us use words that encourage understanding and peace.
our Heavenly Father loves us and desires us to live in peace and harmony. Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace.

scriptures.use: Tell in your own words as the story of people who buried their weapons for peace; older children can read the verse aloud first.
Open your scriptures to it at the close and tell the children that here Jesus promises to give us His peace.
For older children: have one read it aloud, then ask what kind of words Paul wants us to say.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Ulisses Soares
aligned_quotes.text: We can become instruments of His peace in the world.

invitations.text: let us use words that encourage understanding and peace
Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.

takeaways: Jesus is the Prince of Peace.
Kind words build, and I can choose them.
I can use words that bring peace.
act: Say your chosen peace word to someone every day this week.
When you feel upset, stop, take a big breath, and pick a peace word.
If you say something unkind, say “I’m sorry” soon.
Ask Heavenly Father in your prayers to help you use kind words.
music: I'm Trying to Be like Jesus

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: use only two peace words (“Please” and “Thank you”) plus “I’m sorry.” Whisper the word for the child to repeat in the ball game, roll the ball instead of tossing it, and repeat the heart, choices, words actions between activities. Let a helper lead the burying walk.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: have a child read Alma 24:19 and another read Ephesians 4:29 aloud. Let older children make up the pretend moments for the ball game and add longer phrases from Elder Kyungu’s list, such as “We can work this out” or “I am here for you.” Ask: Why is it sometimes hard to say “I’m sorry”? What helps?
